summary: Sets out requirements for extending the IETF Datatracker so ordinary community members and IETF leaders can easily follow the progress of the Internet-Drafts and RFCs they care about. It is an informational requirements document rather than a standard.

plainLanguage.summary: Imagine a website that lets you follow your favorite documents like a mail-tracking page follows a package. This note describes what that tracking features should do so people can see how each document is moving along.

subtitle: Specifications for letting community members track Internet-Drafts and RFCs through their publishing lifecycle.

tldr.problem: IETF participants need to follow the progress of Internet-Drafts and RFCs relevant to their work, but the Datatracker at the time offered only basic search. IETF leadership, working group chairs, and developers needed better ways to track documents, get notifications of status changes, and organize their follow-up work.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 6293 lists a comprehensive set of requirements for enhancing the IETF Datatracker with personal watch lists, Atom feeds and email notifications for document status changes, customizable views, and the ability to track groups of documents by attribute like working group or author.
tldr.outcome: These requirements informed the development of enhanced Datatracker features that allow any community member to create personal lists, receive notifications of document state changes, and filter the Datatracker's view to their interests. Later Datatracker versions incorporated many of these capabilities.

today: RFC 6293 is an Informational RFC documenting requirements for Datatracker enhancements proposed in 2011. Many of these capabilities have since been implemented in later versions of the Datatracker, allowing IETF participants to create watch lists, receive notifications, and customize document views.

sections.title: The Problem: Tracking Documents Through a Long Process
sections.content:
The IETF publishes thousands of Internet-Drafts each year, and hundreds become RFCs. Documents can take months or years to progress through the standards process: a draft must gain working group consensus, pass last-call review, get shepherd write-up, go through IESG review, and finally be published as an RFC. Along the way, the status might change weekly or sit unchanged for months.

IETF community members—working group chairs, area directors, developers implementing protocols, and researchers tracking emerging standards—need to follow many documents at once. They want to know immediately when a document they care about reaches a milestone (like being sent to the RFC Editor) or when new versions are posted. They also want different views of the same information: one person might want to see everything in alphabetical order, another wants recent changes at the top.

The Datatracker, the IETF's official tool for document status, initially offered only basic keyword search. RFC 6293 describes what features it should have to serve the community's tracking needs.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine watching packages being delivered. You care about five packages at once, and you want to know the moment each one arrives at the next stop. You might want to see them in order by delivery date, or by destination, or by what you ordered. The Datatracker should let you do all of that.

sections.title: Lists, Notifications, and Views
sections.content:
RFC 6293 identifies three major capabilities the Datatracker should provide:

Personal lists: Any community member with a Datatracker account should be able to create one personal list of Internet-Drafts and RFCs to follow. The list can hold hundreds of documents. A user should be able to add documents individually by searching, or by attribute (all drafts from a working group, all documents by a particular author, all documents that reference a given RFC). Read-only versions of the list can be shared with others. Working group chairs and area directors should be able to maintain public lists for their WGs or areas.

Notifications: When a document in a list changes status—goes into last call, gets approved, is published as an RFC, or receives an errata—the user should be notified immediately. The RFC requires two types of notifications: one for every status change and another for only 'significant' changes like approvals and publication. Notifications should arrive as Atom feeds (which feed readers fetch automatically) and as email messages, so users can pick their preferred method.

Views: The Datatracker should display the list in sortable columns showing document name, title, current status, working group, date of publication, and other attributes. Users should be able to choose which columns to display and how to sort them—alphabetically, by publication date, by most recent status change, or grouped by the filtering rules used to build the list.
sections.plainLanguage: You make a list of documents. You can add them one by one or say 'add all DNS documents.' When one of your documents changes, you get an email or a feed notification. And when you open the Datatracker page, you can sort your list however you want.

sections.title: Requirements for Lists, Notifications, and Display
sections.content:
Under lists, the RFC requires that adding individual documents be simple, that large lists (hundreds of documents) perform well, that grouping by attributes be easy, and that private information (like private IESG ballot comments) not leak into public lists.

For notifications, the Datatracker needs Atom feeds and mail streams that stay in sync with the list, labeling each notification with which list triggered it so users can disambiguate if they follow multiple lists. Mail should arrive immediately (within an hour), not as daily digests, so users see urgent changes in time.

For display, the RFC lists six useful sort orders: alphabetical by draft name or RFC number, by title, by working group, by publication date, by most recent change, and by most recent significant change. Users should be able to set date flags on documents ('I expect a new version by Friday') and highlight documents changed in the last 1, 2, or 7 days so they can spot what is moving.

The RFC also requires the ability to export the list as a machine-readable file so users can process it with their own tools.
sections.plainLanguage: You should be able to add documents easily. Notifications should arrive fast. You should see your documents in any order you want. And you should be able to download your list and use it in your own programs.

sections.title: Who Benefits and Why
sections.content:
The RFC illustrates several real use cases. A working group chair tracks all drafts from his WG and also all related drafts from other WGs that might affect his work. An area director follows hundreds of drafts in her area plus drafts in other areas that are related to hers. A developer implementing DNS wants to follow not only DNSEXT WG drafts but also any draft that mentions DNS, including individual submissions and IRTF research group work, so she spots new requirements early. An IETF participant might want to follow the shepherding progress of a specific area director to see what he is prioritizing.

For each of these people, the Datatracker's search tool is not enough: they need a saved list they check regularly, notifications to alert them to changes, and the ability to customize what they see. RFC 6293 documents these needs to guide development of the Datatracker's new features.
sections.plainLanguage: A WG chair needs to watch drafts from five other working groups that affect her work. A developer building DNS software needs to see any draft mentioning DNS. An area director has a hundred drafts to oversee. They all need a tool that remembers their list and tells them what changed.

sections.title: Privacy and Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC notes that tracking activity itself can reveal sensitive information: if someone sees you are watching a particular document, they may infer your interests or future plans. This argues for keeping watch lists private by default, allowing users to share read-only versions only by choice.

The RFC also flags risks inherent in web applications with authentication and stored user data: cross-site scripting attacks, session hijacking, and access control bugs. Implementations need strong security practices around account management, password storage, and input validation.

Private information in the Datatracker—such as private comments in IESG ballots—must never be included in public list views, even if a user accidentally grants read access to a list.
sections.plainLanguage: If I make my watch list public, people can guess what I am working on, so lists should be private. Also, hackers might try to steal passwords or read other people's lists, so the tool needs to be secure.
